clue.text: Fellow taking rent in flowers?

definitions.note: A chaplet is a single garland, so the plural 'flowers' describes what it is made of rather than matching its number; the question mark flags the looseness.

parts.note: a chap is an everyday word for a man or fellow
to let a room is to take rent for it

explanation.surface: A tenant who pays his rent in bunches of flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: CHAPLET is CHAP followed by LET; the solver has to see that 'taking rent' describes what a landlord does when letting.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaplet is a wreath or garland worn on the head, typically woven from flowers.

clue.text: Bird has broken bean plant

parts.note: a female fowl

indicators.note: something broken has its parts disordered, so the next word's letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A bird has damaged a bean plant in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bean plant' looks like one item; the definition is just 'plant'.
explanation.definitionFit: Henbane is a poisonous plant of the nightshade family.

clue.text: Might get piano pieces for Wroe

indicators.note: something in pieces has been broken up, so the letters are put back together in a different order

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly
the name supplies the remaining letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Wroe might be given some piano pieces to play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might' looks like a verb of possibility; it is the noun meaning strength.
explanation.definitionFit: Might as a noun means strength or force, which is power.

clue.text: I'd fill in the result — it's obvious

indicators.note: to fill in is to go inside something, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: 'in the event' means as it turned out, so an event is an outcome or result
the contraction with its apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone says they would complete the result because it is plain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fill in' reads as completing a form, but it means insert. 'In the event' means as it turned out, which is why an event can be a result.
explanation.definitionFit: Evident means plain to see or clearly apparent, the same as obvious.

clue.text: This kind of gamble, in short, is without point

parts.note: a gamble on the markets is a speculation, cut down to its usual abbreviation

indicators.note: 'without' in its old sense of 'outside', so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: taken as written; it is the outer piece
a point of the compass, here East

explanation.surface: A betting tip dismissed as a pointless sort of wager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without point' reads like 'pointless', but here 'without' means outside and the point is a compass direction. Spec is the usual short form of speculation.
explanation.definitionFit: A species is a kind or sort of thing, and 'this kind' stands for the noun.

clue.text: Show gets cut without publicity

indicators.note: 'without' in its old sense of 'outside', so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: to pare is to cut or trim
an ad, short for advertisement, is a piece of publicity

explanation.surface: A show is cut short because it was not advertised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without publicity' reads as 'unadvertised'; here 'without' means around, so the publicity sits inside the cut.
explanation.definitionFit: To parade is to display or show off, and a parade is also a public show or procession.

clue.text: Kind of card?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: nature or sort, as in something's essential quality
second meaning: an eccentric, amusing person, as in 'he's a real card'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind of card' suggests a greeting or playing card. A card is also old slang for an eccentric person.
explanation.definitionFit: Character means nature or kind, and a character is also an odd, entertaining person, which is what 'a card' means.

clue.text: Stone gets the dram Lee mixed

indicators.note: mixed things are jumbled together, so the preceding letters are rearranged

parts.note: a measure of whisky and a surname together supply the letters

explanation.surface: A man called Stone is served Lee's mixed drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stone' reads as a person's name; it is a gemstone.
explanation.definitionFit: An emerald is a precious green gemstone, a kind of stone.

clue.text: Compiler of a meaningful work?

parts.note: surface reading: an author of a profound, significant book
setter's reading: a book that is literally full of meanings, one for each word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Meaningful' suggests significant; read literally, the work is full of meanings, a dictionary.
explanation.definitionFit: A lexicographer writes and compiles dictionaries, books that give the meanings of words.

clue.text: Bowler taken for a white man

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a famous English fast bowler of the 1960s and 70s, John ___
second meaning: the stuff you gather to build a white figure in the garden in winter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowler' looks like the hat; it is the England cricketer John Snow, a fast bowler. The second half is loose: it describes the material taken to make a snowman.
explanation.definitionFit: John Snow bowled for England, and snow is the white material from which a snowman is built.

clue.text: Something that made the party go by ship?

definitions.text: Something that made the party go by ship?

parts.words: Something that made the party go
parts.note: surface reading: a remark or game that gets a social gathering going
setter's reading: a vessel that clears a channel through frozen sea, so a party of travellers can go on

explanation.walkthrough: An icebreaker is both a remark that loosens up a party and a ship built to smash through ice so others can sail.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names an opening activity that warms up guests and also a strengthened vessel that cuts through polar ice.

clue.text: Playwright demands sound port in Wales

indicators.note: 'sound' asks for a word that is said the same as the place named next

parts.note: Barry is a port town in South Wales, near Cardiff

explanation.surface: A dramatist insists on visiting a Welsh harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: J. M. Barrie wrote Peter Pan; his surname is said exactly like Barry, the docks town in the Vale of Glamorgan. 'Demands' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. Barrie was the Scottish dramatist who wrote Peter Pan, so his surname names a playwright.

clue.text: Old craft of the countryman

parts.note: the first part of the word names a country, here the subcontinent's largest nation
the end of the word, taken as written

explanation.surface: A traditional skill practised by someone who lives in the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Countryman' must be split: a country plus MAN. 'Craft' reads as a skill but means a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: An Indiaman was a large sailing ship of the East India trade, a vessel of a bygone era.

clue.text: Feeling welcome in Fleet Street?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a physical perception, such as warmth or pain
second meaning: a startling news story, the kind London's newspaper district loved

explanation.walkthrough: Fleet Street is the London street that housed the national newspapers, so it stands for the press. A sensation is a perception and also a story that causes a stir.
explanation.definitionFit: A sensation is a bodily perception, and also a startling event or story that newspapers seize on.

clue.text: Old sailor appears to retaliate in gun battle

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a seasoned seaman, especially one who has crossed the equator
second meaning: to fire artillery rounds back at the enemy, read as two words

explanation.walkthrough: Split into two words, the answer is an instruction to return artillery fire; whole, it is sailors' slang for a veteran.
explanation.definitionFit: A shellback is a nautical term for an experienced old sailor, and to shell back is to answer bombardment with bombardment.

clue.text: Room for boss and youth leader

parts.note: a boss is a raised knob or stud on a surface

indicators.note: a leader comes at the front, so only the opening letter of the word is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: An office for the manager and the head of the youth club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' wants to be a manager; it is the ornamental knob, as on a shield.
explanation.definitionFit: A study is a room set aside for reading, writing or working.

clue.text: Agent's for a confectionery cargo apparently

definitions.note: The answer is plural; the printed apostrophe reads as a slip for 'Agents', the plural noun the answer matches.

indicators.note: a cargo is carried inside a vessel, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: first half of the usual abbreviation for a steamship, the vessel carrying the load
a sweet baked pastry from the confectioner's shop
second half of the steamship abbreviation, closing round the load

explanation.surface: A spy ring operating under cover of a shipment of sweets.
explanation.walkthrough: SS, the steamship, carries PIE as its cargo. This parse is the likeliest reading of a loosely worded clue rather than a certain one.
explanation.definitionFit: Spies are secret agents who gather intelligence for a government.

clue.text: Former state of the quiet country

parts.note: p is the musical marking piano, meaning quietly
the largest country in the world

explanation.surface: A former nation that was once a peaceful land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quiet country' reads as a calm rural place; it is P plus a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Prussia was a German kingdom and state that was dissolved after the Second World War.

clue.text: Poor Peter goes to ceremony appearing tense

indicators.note: something poor is in bad shape, so the name that follows is rearranged

parts.note: the name, whose letters are rearranged
a rite is a formal ceremony

explanation.surface: Unhappy Peter attends a ceremony looking nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' reads as nervous; it is the grammar term.
explanation.definitionFit: The preterite is the grammatical past tense, describing a completed action.

clue.text: A number round Spithead appear dry

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: a number, three tens

indicators.note: the head of a word is its front, so only its opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of the place name

explanation.surface: Many people around Spithead, the Solent anchorage, look parched.
explanation.walkthrough: Spithead is a stretch of water off Portsmouth, but the clue splits it: 'head' takes the front letter of 'Spit'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thirsty means in need of a drink, so dry in the sense of parched.

clue.text: Poet is an unusually smooth Pole

indicators.note: unusually means not in the normal way, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: the word whose letters are rearranged
the North Pole, abbreviated N

explanation.surface: A writer is a remarkably suave man from Poland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' reads as a Polish man; it is a magnetic or geographic pole. James Thomson wrote The Seasons and 'Rule, Britannia!'.
explanation.definitionFit: James Thomson was an eighteenth-century Scottish poet, author of The Seasons.

clue.text: You won't have to work on this!

definitions.text: You won't have to work on this!

parts.note: surface reading: a day off or a holiday
setter's reading: the phrase 'on ___' for workers who have downed tools in a dispute

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a promise of a holiday; the setter means the idiom for workers who are out in protest.
explanation.definitionFit: Workers on strike refuse to work as a protest, so while it lasts nobody does any work.

clue.text: The mark of a finished writer?

definitions.text: The mark of a finished writer?

parts.words: The mark of a finished writer
parts.note: surface reading: the hallmark of an accomplished, polished author
setter's reading: the punctuation a writer puts down when a sentence is finished

explanation.walkthrough: 'Finished' suggests polished and 'mark' suggests a trait; read literally, it is the punctuation mark set down at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A full stop is the punctuation mark that ends a sentence, the point where the writer has finished.

clue.text: Roundhead was one going to the right school

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
R is the standard abbreviation for right
the famous English public school near Windsor

explanation.surface: A Parliamentarian who attended the correct, smart school.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Ireton was a Parliamentarian general and Cromwell's son-in-law. 'The right school' reads as the posh one, which Eton is, but 'the right' gives only R.
explanation.definitionFit: Roundheads were supporters of Parliament in the English Civil War, and Ireton was one of their leading commanders.

clue.text: Man is somebody upset ting the church

indicators.note: the printed line splits 'upsetting'; in a down entry upsetting turns the word over, so it reads from the bottom

parts.note: 'one' as a pronoun means somebody
CH is the standard abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A man is someone who causes trouble in the church.
explanation.walkthrough: Enoch is a man of the Bible, father of Methuselah, which makes 'Man' a fair if wide definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Enoch is a man's name, borne by the biblical patriarch who was the father of Methuselah.

clue.text: Is friend abroad sent to reorganise restaurants?

parts.note: the French for 'is', taken abroad along with the next word

indicators.note: reorganising puts things in a new order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: French for friend
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A friend overseas has been dispatched to overhaul some eateries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' covers both 'Is' and 'friend', turning them into French. The question mark admits that an estaminet is a humble café-bar rather than a restaurant.
explanation.definitionFit: An estaminet is a small French café selling drinks and simple meals, so they are modest eating places.

clue.text: Some hero's saddle from a Greek mount

indicators.note: 'some' asks for just a part of the words that follow, a run of letters within them

parts.note: the letters run on from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Part of a hero's saddle taken from a horse in Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' wants to be a horse, which goes with the saddle; it is a mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: Ossa is a mountain in Thessaly, which in myth the giants piled on Pelion.

clue.text: Statesmen having some pull?

parts.note: surface reading: politicians with influence
setter's reading: men from the United States, whose nickname begins with a word meaning a sharp tug

explanation.walkthrough: Statesmen reads as politicians; it means men of the States. Their nickname opens with YANK, a sharp pull, which is the 'some pull' they have.
explanation.definitionFit: Yankees is the informal name for Americans, people from the United States.

clue.text: Joiners from a happy-go lucky firm?

definitions.text: Joiners from a happy-go lucky firm?

parts.words: Joiners from a happy-go lucky firm
parts.note: surface reading: carpenters employed by a carefree company
setter's reading: the punctuation marks that link the words of this phrase

explanation.walkthrough: Joiners reads as carpenters; the joiners are the punctuation marks that hold 'happy-go-lucky' together.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyphens are punctuation marks that join words into compounds, so they are literal joiners.
